query_text: Write the history of a colour.

content.text:
## A Brief History of Blue

Blue is the colour of distance.

It is the colour of the sky, which can never be touched, and of the sea, which changes the closer you come to it. For much of human history, blue was everywhere in nature but strangely absent from human art, language, and symbolism. It took people a long time to make blue their own.

In prehistoric cave paintings, artists used reds, browns, blacks, and yellows made from earth, charcoal, and minerals. Blue is rare in these early images, not because ancient people could not see it, but because stable blue pigments were difficult to find. Unlike ochre or soot, blue did not lie ready in the hand.

One of the earliest great blues was born in ancient Egypt. Around the third millennium BCE, Egyptian craftsmen created **Egyptian blue**, often considered the first synthetic pigment. Made from silica, copper, lime, and an alkali, it produced a brilliant blue used in tombs, statues, and decorative objects. For the Egyptians, blue was associated with the heavens, the Nile, fertility, rebirth, and divine protection. The hair and beards of gods could be painted blue, suggesting something eternal and otherworldly.

Elsewhere, blue remained precious. In the ancient Mediterranean world, it did not always enjoy high status. The Greeks and Romans often preferred white, red, black, and purple. Blue could be associated with foreigners, barbarians, or mourning. Roman authors sometimes described Celtic and Germanic peoples as painting or tattooing themselves blue, making the colour seem wild and uncivilized.

Its fortunes changed dramatically in the Middle Ages.

In medieval Europe, blue rose from obscurity to holiness. The Virgin Mary began to be depicted wearing deep blue robes, especially from the twelfth century onward. This was not merely an artistic choice; it was also an expensive one. The finest blue pigment was **ultramarine**, made from lapis lazuli mined in Afghanistan and transported across vast trade routes. Its name meant “beyond the sea.” It could cost more than gold.

Because ultramarine was so costly, using it signaled devotion, wealth, and importance. A painter might reserve it for Mary’s cloak, the heavens, or the most sacred parts of an image. Blue became a colour of purity, humility, and divine grace.

At the same time, blue entered politics and fashion. The kings of France adopted blue as a royal colour, often decorated with golden fleurs-de-lis. Dyers improved their techniques using woad and later indigo, making blue cloth more available. By the late medieval and early modern periods, blue had become respectable, elegant, and increasingly common.

Then came indigo.

Indigo dye, extracted from plants, had been used for centuries in Asia, Africa, and the Americas. As global trade expanded, indigo became one of the most important dyes in the world. European empires cultivated it in colonies, often through brutal systems of forced or exploited labour. The history of blue cloth is therefore also a history of trade, colonialism, slavery, and resistance.

Blue became the colour of uniforms, workwear, and everyday life. Sailors wore blue. Soldiers wore blue. Labourers wore blue. Eventually, denim — dyed with indigo — turned blue into the colour of modern casual dress. Blue jeans, originally associated with miners, cowboys, and workers, became in the twentieth century a symbol of youth, rebellion, democracy, and global culture.

Science also transformed blue. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, chemists discovered and manufactured new blue pigments: **Prussian blue**, **cobalt blue**, **cerulean**, and eventually synthetic ultramarine. These made blue cheaper, brighter, and more accessible. Artists used them to capture atmosphere, shadow, water, and emotion.

For painters, blue became a language of feeling. J. M. W. Turner used it in luminous skies and seas. The Impressionists used blue shadows instead of black. Picasso’s Blue Period turned the colour into an expression of poverty, grief, and loneliness. Yves Klein later made blue almost mystical again with his intense International Klein Blue, treating it as a colour of pure sensation.

Blue also became psychological. In modern English, to “feel blue” means to feel sad, though blue can also suggest calm, trust, cleanliness, intelligence, and stability. Corporations and governments use blue because it appears dependable. Police uniforms, business suits, social media logos, hospital signs, and national flags all rely on its authority.

Yet blue remains full of contradictions. It is the colour of melancholy and serenity, royalty and labour, holiness and bureaucracy, oceans and screens. It can feel natural, but many of its most famous forms are technological triumphs. It suggests freedom, yet it has histories tied to empire and exploitation. It is common now, but it was once rare enough to be treasured like a jewel.

Perhaps this is why blue still holds such power. It began as the colour humans could see but not easily possess. It belonged to the sky, to deep water, to distant mountains, to gods. Over thousands of years, people learned to grind it, dye it, trade it, wear it, worship with it, and mass-produce it.

But blue has never entirely lost its distance. Even now, when it glows from every screen and hangs in every wardrobe, it still carries a trace of the unreachable: the horizon, the atmosphere, the dream of somewhere else.
